                             O R D E R
1. The issues arising for decision in this cluster of petitions require in-depth
consideration upon hearing the parties in full. 
2. Due to paucity of time, it will not be possible for this Bench to hear the

parties finally and deliver its opinion by the end of this month.
3. Re-list  the  special  leave  petitions/contempt  petition  on  1st December,
2026 ‘For Directions’.
4. The present petitions will not be treated as heard-in-part.
5. We make it clear that pendency of proceedings will not preclude the State
Government to look into the grievances of the petitioners and, should in any
individual  case  the  grievance  be  found  to  be  justified  and  his/her  claim  is
acceptable, appropriate relief may be granted to the petitioner concerned. 
6. Interim order, passed earlier, shall continue till the next date of hearing.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH:
1.  We have heard Mr. Rishi Malhotra, learned senior counsel and amicus
curiae, Ms. Geetanjali Mohan, learned counsel appearing for NCTE1 and Mr.
Sourabh  Mishra,  learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the  State  of  Madhya
Pradesh on the question as to whether the Teacher Eligibility Test, apart from
RCI2 qualification, is a mandatory qualification to be possessed by aspirants for
appointment as special teachers to impart training to CwSN3. 
2. Order is reserved.
3. Insofar as recruitment process initiated by the State in terms of the order
dated 7th March, 2025 is concerned, it shall be free to take such process to its
logical conclusion in accordance with law subject to the decision to be rendered
by us on the question noted above. 
4. However, it is clarified that if any candidate has not been selected or is
not  being  considered  for  absorption  as  a  special  teacher,  such  aggrieved
candidate shall be at liberty to pursue his remedy before the jurisdictional High
Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
5. I.A. No. 299680/2026 is an application for impleadment/intervention on
behalf of the applicant – Society. It shall be listed on the next date, indicated
hereafter.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL Nos.   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.17220/2026)
GOPICHAND RAMLAL BISHNOI ..... APPELLANT(S)
            
                   VERSUS
STATE OF MAHARASHTRA ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1.  Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 17.04.2026,
passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Judicature  at  Bombay
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) rejecting the
regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant is an accused in Crime No.445 of 2023,
registered  at  Vimantal  Police  Station,  Pune,  under
1

## Page 53

Section 8(c) read with Sections 21(c), 22(c) and 29 of
the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
(briefly the ‘NDPS Act’ hereinafter).
5. According  to  the  prosecution,  on  24.08.2023,
appellant was apprehended by the police and from his
possession 53.86 grams of mephedrone and 312.60 grams of
heroin were recovered.
6. Appellant was arrested on 24.08.2023 and has been
in custody since then.
7. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submits  that
appellant has no criminal antecedents. He is languishing
in jail for almost 3 years, 3 months now. Though
investigation is complete, trial has not yet commenced.
Therefore, further detention of the appellant would not
be just and proper.
8. Learned State counsel for the respondent-State of
Maharashtra has referred to the averments made in the
counter affidavit filed on behalf of the State and
submits that the contraband recovered from the appellant
is more than the commercial quantity. Therefore, the
rigour of Section 37 of the NDPS Act would kick in.
Unless the appellant can overcome the barrier of Section
37 of the NDPS Act, bail may not be granted by the
Court.
2

## Page 54

9. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received the due consideration of the Court.
10. From the materials on record, it is seen that
appellant is in custody since 24.08.2023, for more than
3  years  now.  The  investigation  was  concluded  on
17.02.2024 whereafter charge sheet was submitted before
the Special Court. Prosecution seeks to rely upon the 21
witnesses to prove its case. It is on record that
charges were framed only on 12.02.2026 i.e., after
almost 2 years since submission of the charge sheet.
Though, more than 9 months have gone by since framing of
charges, the trial has not yet commenced.
11. We further find that on an earlier occasion when
the appellant had approached the High Court for bail,
being Bail Application No.3537 of 2024, the same was
disposed of by the High Court on withdrawal with liberty
to file fresh application after 9 months if the trial
was not concluded by that time.
12. In the impugned order, the High Court has observed
that mere lack of progress in the trial cannot be a
ground to consider the bail application in view of
statutory restrictions.
13. In so far the present case is concerned, not to
speak of lack of progress in the trial, the trial itself
3

## Page 55

has not commenced after framing of charges 9 months ago
on 12.02.2026.
14. On a query by the Court, learned counsel for the
appellant submits that the delay in framing of charges
and subsequent delay in the commencement of the trial
post framing of charges cannot be attributed to the
appellant as the appellant is in custody.
15. While certainly the statutory restrictions under
Section 37 of the NDPS Act would have to be borne in
mind while considering a plea for bail of a person
accused  of  committing  offences  under  the  NDPS  Act
involving commercial quantity but when a Constitutional
Court is confronted with a situation where trial has not
at all commenced and the appellant continues to remain
in jail as an under-trial for sufficiently long period
of  time,  then  having  regard  to  the  over-arching
constitutional mandate of Article 21 of the Constitution
of India, a balance would have to be struck. However, no
specific time frame can be fixed as to when delay in
commencement of the trial while the accused continues to
languish in jail as an undertrial can be said to
infringe the fundamental right of the accused under
Article  21.  It  all  depends  upon  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case. However, one thing is clear.
When there is breach of Article 21 of the Constitution
of India, Section 37 of the NDPS Act would have to give
4

## Page 56

way. 
16. In the present case, it has been more than 2 and a
half years since conclusion of investigation; 9 months
since charges have been framed with 21 witnesses to be
examined and the trial has not yet commenced while the
appellant remains in jail as an undertrial for more than
3 years.
17. In the circumstances, we are of the considered
opinion  that  further  detention  of  the  appellant
notwithstanding the statutory embargo under Section 37
of the NDPS Act would be constitutionally impermissible.
18.  Accordingly, we  set aside  the impugned  order
passed by the High Court dated 17.04.2026 and direct
that  the  appellant  shall  be  produced  before  the
jurisdictional Special Court within a maximum period of
7 days from today whereafter he shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed
appropriate.
19.  We further direct that appellant shall appear
before the Trial Court on all the dates as may be fixed
by the Trial Court except on such occasions when his
appearance may be exempted by the Court.
20.    Appeal is accordingly allowed.
5

21.   Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

   O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal is preferred by the de
facto complainant,  Chander Pal, who is the
father of the deceased,  Akshay. Respondent
no.1, Rahul @ Vikram, has been directed to be
released on bail under the impugned order
passed by the High Court on the ground that he
is in jail for last about more than 05 years.
3. It is argued that the High Court
ought to have considered all relevant aspects
of  the  matter,  including  the  criminal
antecedents  of  the  respondent  no.1  and
particularly the fact that respondent no.1,
was earlier convicted for committing offence
under  Sections 307/34 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 & Section 25 of Arms Act, 1959 vide

## Page 61

2
judgment dated 08.11.2016 passed in Sessions
Case No. 02 of 30.01.2015 Session Trial No.01
of 30.01.2015 for attempting on the life of
the injured, Akshay, who is the same person
who has been murdered in the present case.
4. Learned  counsel for  the appellant
would further submit that respondent no.1,
Rahul @ Vikram, is a dreaded criminal and is
involved in series of offence yet, the said
aspect of the matter has not been considered
by the High Court.
5. Learned  counsel appearing  for the
respondent no.1,  Rahul @ Vikram, would submit
that while filing the bail petition before the
High Court, custody certificate was submitted
wherein,  the  criminal  antecedents  were
mentioned  therefore,  the  respondent  no.1,
Rahul @ Vikram, is not guilty of concealing
any material fact before the High Court. He
would also submit that respondent no.1 being
in jail for more than 05 years, the judicial
discretion exercised by the High Court ought
not to be interfered with as it involves the
respondent no.1’s right to speedy trial.

## Page 62

3
6. True it is that the right to speedy
trial is always considered to be a facet of
Article 21 of the Constitution of India but,
at  the  same  time,   when  the  accused  in
involved in committing heinous offence, the
right of the accused and the interest of the
society, including the interest of the victim
and his family, is also required to be seen.
7. In  the  case  at  hand,  while
preferring the bail petition before the High
Court, the respondent no.1 made a statement at
two places firstly, in paragraph no. 3(i) and
again at paragraph no.6 of Annexure P-7 that
he is not involved in any other case except
the present case. Thus, the respondent no.1
has concealed his conviction in the previous
case  wherein,  he  has  been  convicted  and
sentenced for attempting on the life of the
same person, Akshay, who is the deceased in
the present case.
8. Not only this, the present crime has
been committed while the respondent no.1 has
been enlarged on bail in the case where he
stands convicted for committing offence under

## Page 63

4
Sections 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
& Section 25 of Arms Act, 1959.
9. From the impugned order passed by
the High Court, it appears that neither the
previous conviction of respondent no.1 was
ever brought to the notice of the High Court
nor the involvement of respondent no.1 in
other criminal cases were placed before the
High Court at the time of hearing of the bail
petition.
10. A criminal, having antecedents and
previous conviction, cannot be released on
bail merely on the strength of his/ her right
to speedy trial. It is the duty of the Court
to maintain balance between the two facets
i.e., right to speedy trial and the societal
interest, by releasing a person on bail while
he is involved in series of offences and
particularly when the bail order has been
secured by making incorrect statement before
the High Court.
11. For all the above stated reasons, we
are of the clear view that the High Court
ought not have released the respondent no.1,

## Page 64

5
Rahul @ Vikram, on bail pending trial.
12. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order
passed by the High Court is set aside and the
respondent no.1, Rahul @ Vikram, is directed
to surrender before the concerned Court within
a week from today.
13. The appeal stands allowed.

O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of the impugned
judgment dated 08.09.2020 passed by the High Court
of Karnataka at Bengaluru in M.F.A. No. 5843 of
2015.
4. The  facts  of  the  case  reveal  that  the
appellant met with an accident on 10.07.2012, which
ultimately resulted in the amputation of his right
leg. A claim petition was preferred before the
Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, which awarded a
1

## Page 68

sum of Rs. 4,20,000/- despite the amputation and
assessment of 50% disability. On appeal, the High
Court enhanced the compensation to Rs. 10,59,000/-
along with interest at the rate of 6% per annum.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant
submits  that  the  appellant  was  earning  his
livelihood as a coconut vendor using a bicycle, and
on account of the amputation of his right leg, he
is rendered incapable of pursuing his vocation and
is surviving on the meager income of his wife who
works  as  a  tailor.  It  is  submitted  that  the
compensation awarded is grossly on the lower side
for a case of amputation and ought to have been
substantially increased by the High Court.
6. Learned counsel has further argued that no
amount whatsoever has been awarded to the appellant
towards procurement and periodic replacement of an
artificial/prosthetic limb, which is required to be
changed after the expiry of every five years. In
support of his submissions, learned counsel has
placed reliance upon the judgment delivered by this
Court reported in (2014) 2 SCC 735 [Syed Sadiq &
2

## Page 69

Ors. vs. Divisional Manager, United India Insurance
Co. Ltd.].
7. On the other hand, learned counsel appearing
for the respondent-State has opposed the prayer for
enhancement, submitting that the High Court has
already adequately enhanced the compensation to Rs.
10,59,000/- with interest, and that the appellant
can still carry on his business as a coconut
vendor. However, learned counsel has not disputed
that no amount has been awarded under the head of
future prosthetic limb replacement.
8. Having heard learned counsel for the parties
at length and upon perusal of the record, keeping
in  view  the  fact  that  the  right  leg  of  the
appellant has been amputated and no compensation
has  been  awarded  towards  prosthetic  limb
replacement, this Court is of the opinion that the
interest of justice would be subserved by enhancing
the total compensation from Rs. 10,59,000/- to Rs.
20,00,000/- (Rupees Twenty Lakhs only), along with
interest at the rate of 6% per annum.
9. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the
3

## Page 70

compensation is enhanced to Rs. 20,00,000/- along
with interest at the rate of 6% per annum.
10. The respondent-State is directed to deposit
the total amount as directed by this Court, within
a period of six weeks from today before the MACT.
11. The claimant shall furnish his bank account
details  to  the  MACT  so  as  to  enable  direct
electronic transfer of the compensation amount into
his bank account.
12. With  the  aforesaid  observations  and
modification, the appeal stands allowed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

Nagar,  Kotwali,  Telibandha  and  Raipur,

of  the  Bharatiya  Nyaya  Sanhita,  2023,
cumulatively.

appellant submits, that the appellant has been
under incarceration for a period of more than 1
year  approximately,  out  of  the  maximum
punishment prescribed for a period of three
years. It is further submitted that from the
same alleged statement made by the appellant,
numerous FIRs have been registered. 
5.  Learned counsel appearing for the respondent -
State  while  vehemently  opposing  the  relief
sought for, submits that the conduct of the
appellant is required to be seen. Even after the

especially, the criminal antecedents, there is
no need for any interference.
6.  Admittedly,  the  appellant  has  been  under

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 694/2024
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH                           Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
RAMVEER SINGH                                         Respondent(s)
ORDER
1. We have heard Mr. Bhupendra Pratap Singh, learned Deputy
Advocate General for the State of Madhya Pradesh and Mr. Prashant
Shukla, learned counsel for the respondent.
2. On 04.08.2026, we had passed the following order:
“1. We have briefly interacted with learned counsel for the
parties.
2. At the outset, learned counsel for the respondent submits that
though respondent was acquitted by the High Court on 24.05.2017,
he remained in jail till 02.10.2022 in connection with his
conviction in other case(s). It was only on 02.10.2022, he has
come out of jail after spending 22 years.
3. In the circumstances, we call upon learned counsel for the
appellant-State of Madhya Pradesh to obtain instructions as to
whether the State would still like to pursue the present appeal
against the respondent.
4. List on 22.09.2026.”
3. Today, Mr. Singh submits that he has instructions to argue the
case on merits.
4. The respondent was convicted by the Court of Special Judge
under The M.P. Dakaiti Aur Vyapharan Prabhavit Kshetra Adhiniyam,
1981 (for short, the MPDVPK Act) in Special Case No. 14/2001 under
1

## Page 96

Sections 364A and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short,
‘I.P.C.’) and under Sections 11 and 13 of the aforesaid MPDVPK Act.
5. Consequent to such conviction, respondent was sentenced to
life imprisonment and a fine of Rs.10,000/- (Rupees Ten Thousand
Only) with a default stipulation.
6. In the appeal filed by the respondent before the High Court of
Madhya  Pradesh,  Bench  at  Gwalior  (briefly,  the  ‘High  Court’
hereinafter), being Criminal Appeal No. 703/2023, the High Court
vide  the  judgment  and  order  dated  24.05.2017  reversed  the
conviction of the respondent by setting aside the judgment and
order of the Special Judge and acquitted the respondent of all the
charges.
7. We have carefully perused the impugned judgment of the High
Court as well as the materials on record.  We find that the High
Court rightly discarded the Test Identification Parade, which was
the only basis to connect the respondent with the offence.  The
view of the High Court is summed up in paragraph 11 of the impugned
judgment which reads as under:
“11. However, it was not important in the case that what was the
name told by the appellant at the time of abduction or what was
his  actual  name.  However,  when  it  is  alleged  that  abductee
Rajendra Prasad Sharma was taken from his house by two persons,
out of them one was appellant Ramveer Singh then the appellant
Ramveer Singh was seen by witnesses Bhagwati (PW-3) and Vinod
Sharma (PW-6). However, no Identification Parade was arranged
against the appellant before Bhagwati (PW-3) and Vinod Sharma (PW-
6) and no reason has been shown as to why such Parade was not
arranged before these two witnesses. Secondly, it is alleged that
the appellant Ramveer Singh was accompanied by one Shivpratap
Singh but the police had arrested one Jag Singh and nothing could
2

## Page 97

be proved against Jag Singh as to whether he was the person who
accompanied the appellant Ramveer Singh to commit abduction of the
victim Rajendra Prasad Sharma. The investigating Officer M.P.
Sharma (PW-9) did not make the situation clear that what steps he
has taken against that second person Shivpratap Singh and what was
the role of accused Jag Singh against whom the charge sheet was
filed and who was acquitted by the trial Court. Under these
circumstances, it appears that tainted investigation was done by
the SHO M.P. Sharma (PW-9).”
8. Elaborating further, the High Court concluded as under:
“17. When the Test Identification Parade is highly doubtful and it
has no much evidenciary value then the victim Rajendra Prasad
Sharma or other witnesses of the prosecution have failed to connect
the appellant with the crime, it is not proved beyond doubt that
the appellant-Ramveer Singh was the person who abducted the victim
Rajendra Prasad Sharma. Hence, in absence of a fair identification,
the appellant Ramveer Singh could not be convicted of the offfence
under Section 364-A of IPC either directly or with the help of
Section 34 and Section 120-B of IPC and consequently he cannot be
convicted of offence under Section 11/13 of MPDVPK Act. The trial
Court has committed an error in convicting the appellant for the
aforesaid offence.”
9. We are of the view that the High Court was justified in taking
the  aforesaid  view  and  in  acquitting  the  respondent.  No
interference is called for.
10. However, while parting with the record, our attention has been
drawn to a finding recorded by the High Court at paragraph 11 as
extracted  supra  that the tainted investigation was done by the
Station House Officer, M.P. Sharma (PW-9).  We clarify that by the
aforesaid observation, what the High Court wanted to convey was
that the investigation was inadequate and was not carried out in a
proper manner for which the respondent had to be given the benefit
of doubt.  It is not a comment on the conduct of PW-9 and nothing
more should be read into it.
3

## Page 98

11. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is dismissed.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.             OF 2026
               [arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 18728 OF 2026]           
 
DHARMENDRA KUMAR DESHMUKH                    APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH                              RESPONDENT
 
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur, by the impugned
judgment  and  order  dated  28th July,  2026,  has  dismissed  the
appellant’s application for regular bail.
3. Appellant was arrested on 21st December, 2025 in connection
with FIR1 No.0300 of 2025 dated 17th September, 2025 registered at
Police Station Mana Camp, Raipur under Sections 317(2), 317(4),
317(5), 111 and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023.
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the parties and
perused the materials on record which includes the counter affidavit
of the respondent.
1 First Information Report

## Page 146

2
5. Appellant was not named in the FIR.
6. Police reports (charge-sheet and supplementary charge-sheet)
have  been  filed,  whereupon  charges  have  been  framed  on  5th
September, 2026. Prosecution proposes to record the evidence of
15 witnesses to drive home the charges against the appellant. As
and when trial commences, it will take some time to conclude. 
7. Taking an overall view of the matter, we are of the considered
opinion that the appellant need not be detained in custody any
longer and that he could be admitted to an order for release on bail
pending trial.
8. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and order.
9. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject to furnishing of
bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court and subject to such
other terms and conditions as may be imposed by it.
10. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant  shall  not,  directly  or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to the court.
11. In the event there is any breach of the terms and conditions
for grant of bail, the trial court shall be at liberty to cancel the bail
of the appellant.
12. It is  also ordered that the appellant shall diligently attend
proceedings  of  the  trial,  unless  exempted.  If  he  abstains  from

## Page 147

3
attending the proceedings without justifiable cause, that could also
be seen as breach of the conditions for grant of bail and the trial
court will be free to pass appropriate orders.
13. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant
of bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case.
14.  The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the aforesaid terms.
15.  Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the contempt petitioner. 
2. This  Court  vide  order  dated 30th May,  2024
directed the respondent-alleged contemnor to pay a
lump sum of Rs.5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs) to the
petitioner, to put a quietus to the litigation. 
3. The  petitioner  has  come  forward  with  this
Contempt Petition alleging that the respondent has
paid only a sum of Rs.4,00,000/- (Rupees Four Lakhs)
by  way  of  a  cheque  and  there  is  a  balance  of
Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh) to be paid. 
1

## Page 150

4. Along with this Contempt Petition, reply to the
pleader’s notice, filed on behalf of the original
respondent No.1 is also annexed.  A perusal of the
said reply shows that originally, the High Court vide
order  dated  13th December,  2021,  impugned  in  the
Special Leave Petition, has awarded a lump sum of
Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh) to the petitioner.
The High Court has also observed that since the
originally awarded amount has been already deposited,
an amount of Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh) along
with  proportionate  accrued  interest  should  be
disbursed to the petitioner and the balance amount if
any, would be refunded to the Insurance Company. 
5. It appears that the amount lying in the deposit
has been deducted by the respondent-alleged contemnor
while complying with the order passed by this Court. 
6. In view of the above, we grant liberty to the
petitioner, after due identification, to withdraw the
deposited amount with proportionate accrued interest,
if any. 
7. Accordingly, the Contempt Petition stands closed
in the above terms.

               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Writ Petition(s)(Civil)  No(s).  1296/2026
ABHINAV BHARAT CONGRESS THOUGH ITS 
FOUNDING PRESIDENT PROF DR PANKAJ K PHADNIS Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
NATIONAL HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION 
THROUGH REGISTRAR LAW & ORS. Respondent(s)
(IA No. 312764/2026 - PERMISSION TO APPEAR AND ARGUE IN PERSON)
 
Date : 19-11-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :  Petitioner-in-person
                    
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Application for permission to appear and argue in person is
allowed.
2. The  petitioner,  Abhinav  Bharat  Congress,  through  its
President, Professor Dr. Pankaj K. Phadnis, has invoked the writ
jurisdiction of this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution,
purportedly in public interest, raising various issues, especially
re:  enforcement  of  long-dormant  statutory  mandates  for  the
protection of the rights of children and youth.  The petition rests
on four sets of laws, namely, (i) Protection of Human Rights Act,
1993 (for short, the “1993 Act”); (ii) Commissions for Protection
of Child Rights Act, 2005; (iii) Right to Education Act, 2009; and
1

## Page 166

(iv) the amendment to the Preamble of the RBI Act, 1934 brought in
2016.
3. During the course of hearing, the petitioner, appearing in
person, has primarily highlighted the issue of non-establishment of
District Human Rights Courts as contemplated under Section 30 of
the 1993 Act. It is averred that no such Courts have been
established over the last 33 years, and as a result, victims of
human rights violations, especially the children and youth, are
deprived of access to justice.
4. Section 30 of the 1993 Act provides that, for ensuring speedy
trial of offences arising out of violations of human rights, the
State Government may, with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of
the High Court, by notification, specify for each district a Court
of Session to function as a Human Rights Court for trying such
offences. Section 31 further contemplates the appointment of a
Special Public Prosecutor in such Court to prosecute the violators
of human rights.
5. It may, thus, be seen that under statutory scheme, the Human
Rights Courts can be established by the State Government in
concurrence with the Chief Justice of the jurisdictional High
Court.  Thus, the effective recourse for seeking such relief would
be to approach the concerned State Governments and jurisdictional
High Courts, which are better placed to assess the availability of
requisite infrastructure, suitably sensitized judicial officers,
2

## Page 167

adequate financial resources and other administrative arrangements
necessary for the effective functioning of such Courts. We are,
however, cognizant that relegating the petitioner to approach
different High Courts and State Governments individually may cause
considerable hardship and impede the effective pursuit of the cause
espoused in the writ petition. We are, therefore, of the view that
the  National  Human  Rights  Commission  (NHRC)  would  be  the
appropriate authority to examine the issue comprehensively and
consider the desirability of establishment of District Human Rights
Courts, in different States, wherever warranted.
6. In view of the above, we dispose of this petition with a
request to the Hon’ble Chairman of the National Human Rights
Commission to examine the matter and if, upon such examination, the
Commission finds that the designation of Human Rights Courts would
advance the cause of victims of human rights violations and further
the legislative object underlying the 1993 Act, it may take up the
issue with the concerned State Governments and jurisdictional High
Courts for appropriate consideration. We would appreciate it if the
Commission undertakes this exercise within a reasonable period.
7. As regards the other issues raised in the writ petition, we do
not express any opinion. The petitioner is granted liberty to
submit a comprehensive representation with respect to the other
issues to the competent authorities of the Union of India and/or
the respective State Governments. In the event such representations
are made, the authorities concerned are expected to examine the
3

## Page 168

issues raised therein in accordance with law, having due regard to
the larger public interest involved.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand closed.
(NITIN TALREJA)                            (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION NO. 73 OF 2026
PUNJ LLOYD LIMITED PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
RAMO INDUSTRIES PTE. LTD. RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
ARBITRATION PETITION NO. 74 OF 2026
O R D E R
1. Mr. Ritin Rai, learned senior counsel contends that the
arbitration proceedings had lapsed as the former arbitrator had
recused on 21.12.2020 and the application for appointment of
substituted arbitrator is barred by limitation. He further contends
that the petitioner's submission that they were unaware of such
recusal is not borne out from the records. In rebuttal, Mr. Baya
submits  that  the  limitation  for  making  the  application  for
substituted arbitrator would have to be computed as per Section
60(6)  of  the  Insolvency  and  Bankruptcy  Code,  2016  (IBC)  by
excluding the period during which the moratorium was operating in
respect of the company which the petitioner had been referred to
CIRP under the said Code.  He relies on New Delhi Municipal Council
v.  Minosha India Limited [(2022) 8 SCC 384] to buttress such
submission.
1

## Page 170

2. Having considered the rival submissions of the parties in
light of the law laid down in light of New Delhi Municipal Council
(supra), we are unable to agree with Mr. Rai's contention that
since Paragraph 3(h) of the liquidation order dated 27.05.2022
permitted  the  liquidator  to  follow  up  pending  applications,
including  initiation  of  steps  for  recovery  of  dues  pending
liquidation, the same would stand in the way of deducting the
period of moratorium under Section 60(6) of the IBC. We say so for
the following reason.
3. The said liquidation order at Paragraph 3(d) unequivocally
states as follows: 
“(d). The Order of Moratorium passed under Section 14
of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 shall cease
to have its effect and a fresh Moratorium under Section
33(5)  of  the  Insolvency  and  Bankruptcy  Code  shall
commence;”
4. Paragraph 3(h) of the order reads as follows:
“(h). The liquidator shall also follow up the pending 
applications for their disposal during the process of 
liquidation including initiation of steps for recovery 
of dues of the Corporate Debtor as per law.”
5. A combined reading of clauses 3(d) and 3(h) would make it
amply clear that while the hands of the liquidator had not been
tied  in  following  up  pending  proceedings  or  instituting  new
proceedings for recovery of dues during the moratorium period, the
limitation for institution of such proceedings shall be computed
and would not run during such moratorium period in terms of Section
60(6) of the IBC.
2

## Page 171

6. Given this situation, we are of the opinion that the prayer
for appointment of a substituted arbitrator is within time and the
same is allowed. The respondent(s) is given liberty to raise all
other  issues  before  the  substituted  arbitrator  concerned  in
accordance with law.
7. Mr. Justice Sanjiv Khanna, former Chief Justice of India, is
appointed as the substituted arbitrator. The arbitrator shall
continue the proceedings from the stage that they had already
arrived at and take the same to their logical conclusion.
8. The learned Sole Arbitrator shall be at liberty to fix his/her
fees in consultation with the parties.
9. The petitions stand disposed of.

4. As per the prosecution case, three persons were travelling in
in a car and 20.918 kgs of ganja was recovered from those persons.
Though,  the  quantity  is  slightly  higher  than  the  commercial
quantity, the fact remains that 20.918 kgs was recovered from three
persons. Learned counsel for the appellants argued before this
Court that the appellants are in jail for more than six months and
the trial is not progressing. On the contrary, learned counsel for
the State has vehemently argued that the question of grant of bail
does not arise as commercial quantity i.e. 20.918 kgs of ganja was

recovered from three persons. He has stated that the State shall be

date.

incarceration  of  the  appellants,  we  find  that  their  further
detention in custody is unnecessary; hence, we are inclined to
accept the appeals and grant relief as prayed by admitting the
appellants to an order for grant of bail.
6. Accordingly,  we  set  aside  the  impugned  judgment(s)  and
order(s).

person acquainted with the facts of the cases from disclosing such
facts to the court.

for grant of bail, the trail court shall be at liberty to cancel

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner, a Company, applied under a Request For
Proposal (RFP) dated 30.07.2026 issued by the Madhya Pradesh
Housing & Infrastructure Development Board (MPHIDB) upon
which  they  were  found  disqualified  under  the  Special
Eligibility Criteria at Sr. No.19 of the bid summary. The
technical bid having failed, the petitioner approached the
High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur with a petition
1

## Page 178

under  Article  226  of  the  Constitution  of  India  for
evaluating the technical bid and consider the price bid
along with the technically qualified bidders. The impugned
judgment rejected the prayer and hence the instant Special
Leave Petition. 
2. The RFP is found at Annexure P17, and the subject
Clause reads as under: -
“Special Eligibility Criteria:  
If bidder has completed any project of MPHIDB, with a
delay of more than 1 year attributable to bidder;
bidder shall be disqualified.” 
3. Admittedly, the petitioner had participated in the Rewa
re-densification  project  for  construction  of  Government
Printing Press, which though awarded to the petitioner and
agreement executed on 08.09.2016 with a period of completion
of 24 months, there was considerable delay due to the
estimated cost requiring revision. Eventually, the Printing
Press was completed and on applying for a final completion
certificate, the Executive Engineer attributed two years’
delay  to  the  petitioner  and  imposed  a  penalty  of
Rs.7,30,000/-.  The  petitioner  admittedly  on  12.03.2024
deposited Rs.27,88,442/- including the penalty to facilitate
the final measurement and valuation albeit without admitting
liability. The penalty was imposed, as is evident, based on
Clause 4.1.3, Annexure P2, Construction and Development
Contract with respect to the earlier project. This obviously
disqualified the petitioner from the instant RFP brought out
2

## Page 179

by the MPHIDB for densification of the Bhopal Collectorate.
The petitioner did not challenge the Clause under the RFP
and applied under the same, resulting in the technical
disqualification, which is a foregone conclusion, as per the
RFP issued. 
4. Mr. Maninder Singh, learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the petitioner submits that there was no provision in
the  earlier  agreement  that  delay  would  result  in  a
disqualification forever. Reference is also made to Annexure
P18  which  was  a  communication  dated  21.09.2026,
disqualifying the petitioner in the technical bid based on
Clause 19, Special Eligibility Criteria. It is urged that
such  unconscionable  provision,  debarring  a  contractor
forever due to delay occasioned, cannot be sustained in law.
5. Admittedly, the petitioner succumbed to the order of
penalty issued under the earlier agreement and paid the
amounts  to  the  MPHIDB.  When  the  RFP  was  issued,  the
petitioner could have challenged the clause bringing in a
special eligibility criteria, but they chose to submit their
tender without a challenge to the clause. The provision, as
seen from the RFP applies only to the present RFP. Even in
Annexure P18 the disqualification is only in respect to the
said RFP. It cannot be said that there is a disqualification
forever. 
6. We find absolutely no reason to permit the technical
bid of the petitioner or the financial bid to be opened
insofar as the instant RFP is concerned. 
3

## Page 180

7. However, it is a matter of concern that the petitioner
would be disqualified forever if the MPHIDB intends to bring
in such a provision in every RFP it brings out hereafter.
Hence,  the  petitioner  would  be  entitled  to  file  a
representation before the MPHIDB to absolve the petitioner
from the disqualification hereinafter or at least confine it
to a period. 
8. We  direct  the  MPHIDB  also  to  consider  the
representation  on  its  own  merits  and  ensure  that  a
disqualification in the light of the Special Eligibility
Criteria be brought in, only with respect to a specified
prior  period;  failing  which  it  could  be  termed
unconscionable.  
9. With the above observations and liberty, the Special
Leave Petition stands disposed of.     
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

RAVI KUMAR JANGRA & ANR.                           Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.                              Respondent(s)
Date : 19-11-2026 This petition was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :Ms. Avantika Chaudhary, Adv.
                   Mr. Piyush Singh, Adv.
                   Mr. Nitesh Ranjan- 3551, AOR
                                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioners are home buyers in a project known as ‘Krishna
Housing  Scheme’,  situated  at  Sector-14,  Sohna,  Gurugram.  The
project was launched by respondent No. 4, M/s Raheja Developers
Limited private builder-cum-developer.
2. It appears that a Tripartite Agreement was executed between
the petitioners, the State Bank of India and respondent No. 4
regarding housing loans availed by the petitioners. It is alleged
that the builder-cum-developer failed to honor its commitment as
per the Tripartite Agreement. Although, the disbursement of the
loan was linked to construction progress, the Bank appears to have
made payment to the builder without any corresponding progress in
1

## Page 310

the  construction.   Meanwhile,  respondent  No.  4,  builder-cum-
developer was admitted into CIRP by the National Company Law
Tribunal (for short, “NCLT”) on 21.08.2025. In CIRP proceedings,
the  builder-cum-developer  had  proposed  to  refund  the  amount
deposited by home buyers in six monthly installments.
3. Pending above proceedings, the State Bank of India filed
recovery suits against the Petitioner-home buyers before Commercial
Court, Saket Courts, New Delhi. Consequently, certain ad-interim
directions were issued by the Civil Court regarding payment of
installments by the petitioners to the State Bank of India.
4. In our considered opinion, it is the bounden duty of the
competent Court to first determine the nexus between the builder
and the Bank authorities and examine whether the Bank disbursed the
loan amount to the builder strictly in terms of the Tripartite
Agreement. Unless a categorical finding is returned that the home
buyers are in default, no interim direction regarding payment of
installments can be issued against them.  We, therefore, direct the
Civil Court to not take any coercive action against the petitioners
or similarly placed home buyers without first deciding the above-
mentioned issue.
5. It is clarified that we have not expressed any opinion on
merits of the case and only an ad-interim protection has been
granted to the home buyers against coercive means. All the issues

## Page 312

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CIVIL) NO. 17611 OF 2024)
ALOK KUMAR SUR APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
NATIONAL INSURANCE COMPANY 
LTD. & ANR. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. On 30.08.2007 at 8:10 hours, the appellant was trying to board
a bus bearing Registration No.WB23A/7293. The bus suddenly started
moving in order to overtake another bus of route No. 230. As a
result, the appellant fell down and suffered fracture injuries on
both legs. He was taken to hospital where he was admitted and was
treated for over a month till 19.09.2007. Accordingly, he suffered
a permanent partial disability of 35%. He was working as a Head
Cashier at United Bank of India and was earning a gross salary of
Rs.24,964.85. Assessing these relevant circumstances, the Motor
Accident Claims Tribunal (“MACT”) awarded compensation of Rs.
11,44,987/- with 5% interest per annum from the date of filing of
the application, and in default, to carry a compound interest at
the rate of 9% per annum till realization. On appeal by the
insurance company, the amount came to be reduced by the High Court
to Rs. 2,23,709/- with interest at 5% per annum.
3. We have heard the submissions at the bar. We have also gone
through the impugned judgment.
1

## Page 313

4. The moot issue which weighed with the High Court to reduce the
amount is the fact that the appellant was working as a Head Cashier
and his earning potential had not been adversely affected due to
permanent partial disablement of 35%. We are unable to agree with
such finding of the High Court. The evidence on record clearly show
that the appellant had suffered permanent partial disablement of
35% and was working as a computer operator in the bank.  No
evidence is forthcoming that such disablement had not affected his
efficiency  or  the  possibility  of  his  further  growth  in  the
establishment where he was employed.  The High Court delved in the
realm of speculation and incorrectly reduced the compensation
awarded to the claimant.  
5. Given these circumstances, we set aside the order of the High
Court and restore the order passed by the Tribunal. The appeal is
allowed.              
..........................J.
       (JOYMALYA BAGCHI)
..........................J.
       (V. MOHANA)
NEW DELHI;
NOVEMBER 16, 2026.

and OCI Card of the child. If the same is obtained, the

this Court.

with the ongoing mediation proceedings.

request The Embassy of the United States of America to
expedite the issuance of passport of the minor child,

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                        O R D E R
The trial has progressed, and the examination-
in-chief of PW-1 has been recorded. However, the
cross-examination is yet to take place. According to
the learned counsel appearing for the respondent-
State, there are 28 witnesses to be examined.
1

## Page 421

Admittedly, neither the victim nor the father
of the victim has been examined so far. The other
witnesses of fact have also not been examined. As
such, we are not inclined to grant bail to the
petitioner at this stage.
We, however, direct the Trial Court to make an
endeavour to examine all the witnesses of fact within
a period of four months.
Thereafter, it will be open for the petitioner
to revive his prayer for bail, provided there is no
delay caused attributable to the petitioner in the
conduct of the trial as directed above.
List the matter on 5th  April, 2027.
In the meantime, if the remaining witnesses of
fact have turned hostile or from their statements, it
requires reconsideration of the petitioner’s prayer
for bail, it will be open for the petitioner to apply
for early listing of the matter.

with functioning of the Kunnamkulam Bar Association, Thrissur
District, Kerala (Bar Association). The petitioners before us are
two women advocates. Petitioner No. 1 is seeking membership of the
Bar Association, which has not been processed till date. On the
other hand, Petitioner No. 2 is seeking a declaration of her having
been elected as Joint Secretary of the Bar Association.
3. During  the  course  of  hearing,  learned  counsel  for  the

petitioners has pointed out that vide an order dated 28.10.2026,
passed by the District Judge, Thrissur, the controversy with
respect to the election of the Bar Association has been referred to
the mediation.

at this stage with a direction that the issues raised by the
petitioners herein be also considered and examined by the Committee
of Mediators in terms of the order dated 28.10.2026.
5. If the grievances of the petitioners are not adequately
addressed, liberty is granted to them to approach the State Bar
Council or the jurisdictional High Court, if so required.
6. With liberty aforesaid, the Writ Petition is disposed of.

THE ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA & ORS.        Respondent(s)
(IA No. 337947/2026 - EX-PARTE STAY and IA No. 337946/2026 -
EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.)
 
Date : 19-11-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) : Dr. Alex Joseph- 1928, AOR
                   
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  instant  writ  petition,  purportedly  filed  in  public
interest invoking Article 32 of the Constitution, seeks quashing of
the circular/instructions dated 01.10.2026 issued by the Election
Commission of India (ECI).
2. In sum and substance, the grievance of the petitioner appears
to be that pre-filled enumeration forms are being distributed
without undertaking physical verification of the persons ordinarily
residing in each dwelling house. According to the petitioner, this
has resulted in the inclusion, in the electoral rolls of their
erstwhile places of residence, of persons who have since migrated
and are no longer ordinarily residing there.
1

## Page 579

3. As  an  example,  the  petitioner  has  referred  to  a  draft
electoral roll wherein the name of a voter is stated to have been
included despite the fact that, according to the petitioner, she no
longer ordinarily resides at the address concerned.
4. In our considered opinion, such discrepancies, if any, are
amenable to correction through the prescribed statutory mechanism,
including the filing of objections in Form 7 or by otherwise
bringing the same to the notice of the ECI.  In any case, if there
is any broader deficiency in the overall process, we deem it
appropriate to dispose of this petition with liberty to the
petitioner to forward a copy of this writ petition to the ECI as a
representation.
5. It goes without saying that any suggestions made by the
petitioner for improving the preparation and revision of electoral
rolls shall be duly considered.
6. The Writ Petition is disposed of with pending application(s),
if any.
(NITIN TALREJA)                            (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR
2
